<reason>Both sides argued sharply, but PRO (Side B) made the debate easier to decide. CON's strongest weapon was the "hostage baby" dilemma; PRO answered it honestly in A1 (no stranding, but a slow, litigious, prosecutable route for non-compliant couples) rather than dodging, and gave a plausible pre-conception arithmetic mechanism. CON's counter that "friction is not deterrence" was fair but left its own alternative murky: "refuse the stamp, keep the liability" never squarely rebutted [B1.4]'s relocation point, and PRO's Q1 exposed that refusing licences on standards is close to the motion. Most decisively, PRO turned CON's own week-twenty irreversibility point: every CON remedy (prosecution, immunity for coming forward) arrives after the harm, while the motion's conditions (independent counsel, escrow, single-embryo protocol) arrive before conception and only a "legal only when" regime can impose conditions of entry. CON's closing legitimation/market-expansion argument was its most original contribution but rested on a speculative spillover-to-uncertified-lanes mechanism introduced with full weight only at the end. CON was also clipped in every substantive speech, losing its punchlines. Neither side used fake precision; PRO's India/Thailand/adoption background was ordinary and plausible.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing turn of [A2.7]: CON established that a surrogate at week twenty cannot walk away, and PRO used that exact fact to sort remedies by timing, showing CON's liability-only model is the ex-post tool CON itself said does the least work, while the licence is the only instrument that can withhold entry before harm occurs.</best_rebuttal>
